item.title: Chinese humanoid robot breaks Usain Bolt's 100m dash record at 9.39 seconds
item.description: A humanoid robot named Lightning Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, edging Usain Bolt's record.
item.content:encoded:
The world's fastest man record was shattered on the first day of the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday.

Jamaican Usain Bolt's 100-meter dash record of 9.58 set in 2009 was edged by a Beijing-based X-Humanoid robot named Lightning Bolt, which ran 100 meters at 9:39 seconds before smashing into a blue wall.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone company Honor completed a 100-meter sprint in a record of 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games, the company said, at a peak speed of 14.5 meters per second.

After smashing into the wall, the robots were placed on a stretcher, unlike Bolt, who was able to jog a lap to celebrate human achievement in 2009.

ROBOTS BEAT HUMANS IN HALF MARATHON

The World Humanoid Robot Games, in its second year, features more than 2,000 robots in 51 events and 1,000 competitions like running, table tennis and soccer. The five-day event highlights China's rapid progress in robotics amid a heated tech race with the U.S.

The games, which are taking place in the National Speed Skating Oval built for the 2022 Winter Olympics, opened the same week Beijing was holding the 2026 World Robot Conference, where companies showcased around 3,000 products, including humanoid robots.

CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88 meters, well above the 0.95 meters best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45 meters set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993.

Some spectators at the robot games said they were excited about the humanoid robots’ quickly improving abilities.

Humanoid robots are "evolving rapidly," said Li Yanfeng, an education worker and a Beijing resident.

UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES

"At first, I wasn’t very accepting of artificial intelligence. I was even a bit resistant to it, because of the possibility that it might replace or displace humans," she said. "But now that I see this development is unstoppable, I decided to come and take a look."

"These sports are perfectly normal for humans, but now robots can do them. I find it amazing," said Yang Shangzheng, another spectator.

NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL

Liu Tao, who was watching the games with his son, said he was hoping to see "the best robots China currently has to offer."

This year’s robot games — which the organizer said has 16 countries participating, among them Germany, Japan and the U.S. — also include other events such as weightlifting and tug of war.

The U.S. has stepped up scrutiny of robots from China, which makes the majority of the world's humanoid robots.

President Donald Trump's Federal Communications Commission (FCC) banned imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots, because they "pose unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons."

"I welcome these Executive Branch national security determinations, and I am pleased that the FCC has now added foreign produced advanced robotics and power inverters to the FCC’s Covered List," FCC Chair Brendan Carr wrote in a statement last month. "Following President Trump’s leadership, the FCC will continue to do our part to secure America’s critical supply chains and, with today’s action, the FCC is acting in lock step with our national security agencies to do just that."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Alaska Republicans scramble to educate voters on suspected Dem plant as 'ballot fatigue' threatens race
item.description: Dan Sullivan faces voter confusion from a candidate look-alike sharing his name as Alaska's ranked choice voting system adds complexity to the Senate race.
item.content:encoded:
In addition to fending off a Democratic challenger, Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, is wrestling against confusion caused by a candidate who shares his name — Dan J. Sullivan Jr., an independent — and a shrinking window to clear it up.

Alaska state Sen. James Kaufman, a Republican, said he personally remains worried about conflation between the two.

"I’ve had at least one person say they had to slow down to make sure they didn’t make a mistake. And I can only imagine people who are less engaged in politics — I think it can be confusing," Kaufman said.

Results on Tuesday seem to confirm his hunch.

Sullivan Jr.’s campaign, which has focused on his background as a logger, has meaningfully splintered support from the incumbent Republican candidate in the primary — but not enough to create ambiguity about who the frontrunner was in the primary. Now, the question becomes whether the Sullivan look-alike will have a proportional impact in November, given Alaska’s ranked choice voting system, a larger pool of voters and more time for Republicans to warn voters about the dueling Sullivans.

MORNING GLORY: ALASKA’S 'REAL' SENATOR DAN SULLIVAN STOOD UP OVER CHALLENGER

Former Congresswoman Mary Peltola convincingly led the field on Tuesday, beating out Sen. Sullivan by a 5.4% lead.

Notably, the votes that went to Sullivan Jr. wouldn’t have closed the gap entirely had they been cast for the senator, having received just 2.3%.

Even so, Randy Ruedrich, Republican Party chairman from 2000-2013, believes the confusion is evident.

As a state resident, he pointed out that Alaska’s lone congressman, Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, had received as much support in his own primary as the top non-Democrats vying for the Senate seat: Sen. Sullivan, Sullivan Jr. and Gerald Heikes, a veteran.

"Nick Begich, without all this entertainment, has 60,061 votes. Nick Begich has slightly less Republican votes than these three Republicans together," Ruedrich said.

"There is some obvious crossover."

Ruedrich noted that Alaska has grappled with voter name confusion before. He recalled that, in 2022, little-known Buzz Kelly advanced to a general election when enough voters confused him with Republican Senate candidate Kelly Tshibaka. Tshibaka had been campaigning using just her first name, effectively creating two "Kelly" candidates.

"We had a lady running who was using her first name to identify herself because her last name is a nightmare," Ruedrich recalled. "We’ve had identity issues and confusion in the past."

Ruedrich believes that attempts to muddy the waters also go beyond just Sullivan Jr.’s campaign. He pointed out that this year looks different for Heikes — the Republican with the third-most support on Tuesday and a familiar face in Alaska politics.

"Now, why am I bringing up Heikes? He is a perennial candidate. He has run a number of times, but he's always been unfunded," Ruedrich said.

JUDGE RULES REPUBLICAN WITH SAME NAME AS SEN DAN SULLIVAN CAN STAY ON ALASKA PRIMARY BALLOT

"This year, he has a significant contribution of hundreds of thousands of dollars from a Massachusetts liberal who is contributing to this ultra-conservative Republican, and they're running ads saying that Dan Sullivan is not pro-life; he's pro-abortion."

Heikes has backing from groups like Right for Alaska, which has put roughly $1.2 million up to oppose Sen. Sullivan and $410,000 to support Heikes.

It remains unclear if Heikes will advance to the general election as election results are not final.

One notable difference between Alaska’s top-four jungle primary and its general election is the implementation of ranked-choice voting in November.

Under this system, voters rank their preferred candidates. If their top choice is eliminated, their support passes on to their next-ranked option. While supporters of the process argue it expands voters' power and greatly increases the influence of candidates that may not otherwise be a top choice, critics believe it also introduces confusion.

Kaufman fears that some voters won’t bother to fill out both the "Sullivans" on the ballot to cover their bases.

He believes there are still some voters in Alaska, especially Republicans, who refuse to use the system, citing disagreements with its implementation.

"Some people have a pretty strong traditionalist perspective: one person, one man, one vote," Kaufman said.

"And so, the ballot fatigue where people just don’t rank because maybe they disagree with it; there’s a pretty strong segment of the population here that just patently disagrees with the rank-choice voting system we ended up with. And they don’t necessarily believe in utilizing it."

Both Kaufman and Ruedrich remain unclear about how much confusion the Sullivan Jr. campaign will add in November, but noted that Republicans will likely make it a focus to highlight the issue in the remaining months of the campaign.

SAME-NAME CANDIDATE DISQUALIFIED FROM KEY SENATE RACE OVER ALLEGED DEM SCHEME TO CONFUSE VOTERS

"It has had some blog coverage and some social media coverage," Ruedrich said.

"I expect that’s going to go up significantly to get more people to understand what the problem really is," he added.

In terms of proportionality, Sullivan Jr.’s most notable support came from his hometown, Petersburg Kupreanof. There, he received 66 votes to Sen. Sullivan’s 213 votes — roughly 33% of the incumbent’s support.

Sullivan Jr.’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Tom Hanks put 'Band of Brothers' stars in their place during boot camp 'mutiny,' Neal McDonough reveals
item.description: Neal McDonough reveals how Tom Hanks arrived by helicopter to deliver a powerful speech that ended a cast mutiny during "Band of Brothers" boot camp.
item.content:encoded:
"Band of Brothers" star Neal McDonough recalled how Tom Hanks put the show's cast in their place during the grueling boot camp that they underwent prior to filming.

McDonough, 60, co-starred in the hit 2001 HBO war drama miniseries, which was executive produced by Hanks, 70, and Steven Spielberg, 79.

"Band of Brothers" told the story of the real-life soldiers of Easy Company, part of the U.S. Army’s 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division, as they fought their way across Europe during World War II.

NEAL MCDONOUGH SAYS HOLLYWOOD LABELED HIM A ‘RELIGIOUS NUT,’ COST HIM HIS CAREER AND HOME

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, McDonough recalled how the actors rebelled during the production's intense boot camp before Hanks arrived by helicopter and delivered a powerful message that they "never forgot."

"About five days into boot camp, there was a mutiny," McDonough said on the red carpet at Televerse 26 in Los Angeles.

"All of a sudden, my teeth are knocked out by a .30 cal and I broke my toe, and a slew of other guys was getting tortured," he continued.

"The American guys really loved it," he added with a laugh. "But, there was this mutiny going on. They were like, 'This isn't what we signed up for.'"

TOM HANKS JOKINGLY SWIPES MS NOW'S VIEWERSHIP WHILE APPEARING LIVE ON-AIR WITH REPORTER

"All of a sudden, this helicopter shows up in the middle of our Army base and out walks Tom Hanks with his beard down here and his ‘Cast Away’ hair," McDonough recalled, referencing Hanks' starring role in the survival drama "Cast Away."

WATCH: Tom Hanks arrived by helicopter to confront ‘Band of Brothers’ boot camp ‘mutiny,’ co-star says

"And he got us all attention, and he says, ‘Look, we all owe it to everyone in Easy Company, and everyone in World War II, to work our hardest because they gave their lives for our freedoms. The least we can do is work our tails off to tell the truth as hard as we can so we give honor to those men and women,'" McDonough remembered of Hanks.

McDonough told Fox News Digital that the two-time Oscar winner's words completely shifted the cast's mindset toward portraying "Band of Brothers'" real-life heroes.

"Telling you after that, we were all brainwashed," he said before clarifying, "I'm not sure brainwashed is the right word."

STEVEN SPIELBERG ADMITS HE'S BEEN CONVERTED ON UFOS, SAYS HE BELIEVES THE BELIEVERS

"Where we all realized Tom was right," McDonough continued. "They lived, breathed, and died for what we have this day, freedom. None of us forgot about that, and as soon as the show came out, we realized Tom was right the whole time."

"He knew it was going to be a massive hit. Stephen knew it would be a big hit. We were just lughead actors who were doing our jobs. And then when it came out, and it was the hit that it became, and it is still 25 years later, it just boggles my mind how fortunate every single one of us were to be cast in the show."

ADRENALINE-PACKED PREVIEW RELEASED FOR UPCOMING D-DAY FILM 'PRESSURE,' FEATURES LOADED CAST

McDonough played 1st Lt. Lynn "Buck" Compton, a real-life platoon leader in Easy Company. Compton fought in major WWII campaigns, including D-Day and Operation Market Garden and was wounded during fighting in the Netherlands.

"Band of Brothers" also starred Damian Lewis, Ron Livingston, Donnie Wahlberg, David Schwimmer, Michael Cudlitz and Scott Grimes, while future stars including Tom Hardy, Michael Fassbender and James McAvoy appeared in smaller roles.

The 10-part miniseries was based on historian Stephen E. Ambrose’s 1992 nonfiction book, "Band of Brothers" and was created by Hanks and Spielberg, who had previously collaborated on the acclaimed 1998 World War II film "Saving Private Ryan." Writer Erik Jendresen also helped lead the series adaptation.

Hanks also directed episode five, titled "Crossroads," and had a brief, uncredited cameo.

MATT DAMON WAS 'PUSHED TO THE LIMIT' WHILE FILMING 'THE ODYSSEY,' DETAILS GRUELING PHYSICAL DISCOMFORTS

"Band of Brothers," which premiered in September 2001, earned widespread critical acclaim and received multiple awards, including seven Emmys and a Golden Globe.

The series was extensively praised for its gritty realism and attention to historical detail. The boot camp that the actors underwent was specifically intended to help them move, behave and bond more convincingly as soldiers.

WATCH: Neal McDonough went to hospital as his ‘Band of Brothers’ character after brutal boot camp injury

While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough recalled how the "brutal" boot camp was led by Dale Dye, retired U.S. Marine Corps captain, Vietnam War veteran, actor and longtime Hollywood military technical advisor.

McDonough explained that the boot camp was more challenging for some actors than others.

"I'm a knucklehead. I love that kind of stuff. Those two weeks felt like three months for a lot of guys," he said. "And it was tough."

McDonough told Fox News Digital that Dale intentionally "allowed himself to be the common enemy" to the actors during the series' production.

"We all hated his guts, because he pushed us all to the brink," he recalled of Dye. "And it wasn't until about a quarter of the way through filming that we realized he was putting on an act so we could all gel together as a unit."

"There are a few men on this planet that I love like I love Dale Dye because he allowed himself to be that guy and 'Band of Brothers' would not be ‘Band of Brothers’ were not for him,'" McDonough added.

In additional to serving as the senior military advisor for "Band of Brothers," Dye also played Col. Robert F. Sink, the real-life commander of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, in the series. Dye is one of Hollywood’s leading military advisors and has previously worked on movies, including "Platoon" and "Saving Private Ryan," and TV shows, including "The Pacific" and "Masters of the Air."

Despite the cast's eventual gratitude for Dye's dedication and methods, the physically demanding boot camp took a toll on the actors. McDonough recalled that Dye even considered suspending the training after several actors suffered injuries. The "Minority Report" star remembered that he was hit in the mouth with a ".30 cal" shortly after.

"I heard him say, ‘If one more guy gets hurt, then I might shut this whole thing down.’ That afternoon, I got hit," McDonough said. "We're enveloping this one house. Guy comes out with a .30 cal, boom, smashes my teeth, blood all the way down here."

McDonough remembered that his co-star Shane Taylor, who played medic Eugene "Doc" Roe, became incredulous when he asked him for medical treatment after the injury.

"I said, ‘Doc, get over here, stitch me up,'" McDonough said.

McDonough recalled Taylor replying, "'I'm not a doctor, I'm an actor,'" to which he said he responded, "'I don't care, just stitch me up.'"

"So he stitches me up in front of everybody, and then two or three days later, it's so infected, that Dale's like, ‘You need to go to the hospital.’ And I knew he was sweating," McDonough said. "But at the time, I was just gung ho, because of what Tom said."

McDonough recalled that he went to the hospital, where he provided his character's name and information instead of his own.

"I knew it was socialized medicine, I knew. But I needed to have ‘Lynn Compton’ on that report, not ‘Neal McDonough,’" he said.

McDonough told Fox News Digital that the doctor who treated him was horrified when he saw his infected mouth.

"The doctor's like, 'Oh gosh, that's awful, this is terrible,'" he recalled. "So they shaved it all off, they cleaned it up, stitched me up."

WATCH: ‘Band of Brothers’ stars ‘hated’ boot camp leader before discovering it was all an act, Neal McDonough says

The "Yellowstone" alum told Fox News Digital that he visited Dye afterward. He remembered Dye becoming emotional when presented with McDonough's hospital paperwork, realizing how deeply the actor had committed to his portrayal of Compton.

"I get back to the barracks at 4 o'clock in the morning, I knock on his door, he's sitting there waiting. I put it down there [and said] ‘Sir.’ And he looks at it, and he looked at me and tears welled up in Dale's eyes," McDonough said.

"And I knew that I did a right thing for Easy Company and the whole movie, and after that, we became like that," he continued. "But that was probably the most difficult moment of the boot camp for me."

McDonough met the real Compton prior to filming the show and the two developed a friendship that lasted until the former soldier's death in 2012. He previously described Compton as "another father figure" in his life, and said he nicknamed his son Morgan "Little Buck" in Compton’s honor. McDonough also attended Compton’s 90th birthday celebration and later gave a eulogy at his funeral.
